narrative: The model estimated your probability of bad credit at 39.0%. That is not a prediction that you will default, but it was above the bank’s denial threshold, so your application was declined. The strongest factor in the assessment was your savings information: because it was recorded as unknown or none, it actually worked in your favor and lowered the estimated risk. The second strongest factor was your checking-account status; having no checking-account status also pushed the estimate toward good credit. The main adverse factor among the top three was the amount you requested. You asked for 7,980 DM, while approved applicants average about 3,020 DM, so the larger request pushed your risk estimate upward. In other words, the two strongest items the model looked at were protective, but the high requested amount and other risk factors in your profile were enough to leave the overall risk above the bank’s cutoff. Next, ask the bank whether a smaller loan amount, additional documentation of savings or checking-account activity, or a guarantor or co-applicant would change the decision. Reducing the request toward the typical approved range and providing clearer financial documentation would be the most direct ways to strengthen a future application. You may also ask what specific threshold applied and whether you can appeal with updated information.
